In the Cretaceous, at the time of the dinosaurs
In the ice age of the last 2 million years
100452.e: In the Precambrian there were hardly any animals that could graze on microbial mats. Stromatolites therefore covered large shallow seas.
100452.m: The heyday of stromatolites was in the Precambrian.

100453.e: Cyanobacteria form mats that trap sediment and precipitate lime. They carry out photosynthesis and brought oxygen into the atmosphere early on.
100453.m: Stromatolites are built mainly by cyanobacteria.

100454.q: Which features make a fossil a good index fossil?
a: A short lifespan of the species and a wide distribution
A long lifespan of the species and rare occurrence
Large body length and life on land
100454.e: A species that existed only briefly pins down the time precisely. Wide distribution and abundance allow layers to be compared at places far apart.
100454.m: Good index fossils lived briefly, were common and widespread.

100455.q: Which extinct cephalopods with a bullet-shaped calcite rostrum, popularly called ‘thunderbolts’, serve as index fossils of the Jurassic and Cretaceous?
100455.e: Usually only the solid, pointed calcite rostrum of a belemnite is preserved. Their species changed quickly, which makes them useful time markers.
100455.m: Belemnites left behind the thunderbolts as index fossils.

100456.q: Which colony-forming marine animals are important index fossils of the Ordovician and Silurian?
100456.e: Graptolites drifted in the plankton and so spread across all oceans. Their species changed rapidly, which allows a fine division of time.
100456.m: Graptolites divide up the Ordovician and Silurian.

100457.q: Why are tiny microfossils particularly good index fossils?
a: They are very common, even in small rock samples
They are especially large and easy to see
They occur in only one single place
100457.e: A handful of rock can contain thousands of microfossils. This allows precise dating even in drill cores.
100457.m: Microfossils are common and practical index fossils.

100458.q: Which coin-shaped single-celled organisms are index fossils of the Eocene and also occur in limestones of the Swiss Alps?
100458.e: Nummulites are large foraminifera with a lens-shaped shell. The name comes from the Latin ‘nummulus’, little coin.
100458.m: Nummulites are the coin stones of the Eocene.

100459.q: Which English geologist realised around 1800 that rock layers can be compared by their fossils?
100459.e: William Smith formulated the principle of faunal succession. In 1815 he published the first geological map of the whole of England and Wales.
100459.m: William Smith discovered the order of fossils in the layers.

100460.q: What is the method of dating rock layers using fossils called?
100460.e: Biostratigraphy uses index fossils to divide layers into zones. Radiometry, by contrast, measures the decay of radioactive isotopes.
100460.m: Biostratigraphy dates layers by their fossils.

100461.q: What kind of age does an index fossil on its own provide?
a: The exact date of the animal’s death
100461.e: An index fossil shows whether a layer is older, younger or the same age as another. Figures in years only come from combining it with radiometric dating.
100461.m: Index fossils give a relative age.

100462.q: What is a galvanic cell called that can be recharged by applying an external voltage?
100462.e: In a rechargeable battery (secondary cell), the cell reaction is reversible. During charging, it runs in the opposite direction as an electrolysis.
100462.m: An accumulator is a rechargeable galvanic cell.

100463.q: What is the polarity of the anode in a galvanic cell?
100463.e: Electrons are released at the anode and build up there. That is why it is the negative terminal in a galvanic cell.
100463.m: In a galvanic cell, the anode is the negative terminal.

100464.q: What is the job of the salt bridge in a galvanic cell?
100464.e: Ions move through the salt bridge and balance the excess charges in the half-cells. Without it, the current would stop at once.
100464.m: The salt bridge completes the circuit through moving ions.

100465.q: What is the galvanic cell made of a zinc half-cell in zinc sulphate solution and a copper half-cell in copper sulphate solution called?
100465.e: John Frederic Daniell developed this cell in 1836. It is the classic school example of a galvanic cell.
100465.m: The Daniell cell combines a zinc and a copper half-cell.

100466.q: What is the nominal voltage of an AA alkaline manganese battery?
100466.e: The cell of zinc and manganese dioxide in potassium hydroxide solution gives a nominal voltage of 1.5 V. Rechargeable NiMH cells of the same size give only about 1.2 V.
100466.m: An alkaline manganese cell gives 1.5 volts.

100467.q: Who built the first battery around 1800 from stacked zinc and copper discs with soaked cardboard?
100467.e: Alessandro Volta presented the voltaic pile in 1800. The unit volt is named after him.
100467.m: The voltaic pile is considered the world's first battery.

100468.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a galvanic cell?
100468.e: A spontaneous redox reaction is split in space so that the electrons flow through an external conductor. In this way, chemical energy is converted directly into electrical energy.
100468.m: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy.

100469.q: In which direction do the electrons flow in the external wire of a Daniell cell?
a: From the zinc to the copper
From the copper to the zinc
They do not flow at all
100469.e: Zinc is less noble and gives up electrons. These flow through the wire to the copper electrode, where copper ions are reduced.
100469.m: In the wire, electrons flow from the less noble to the more noble metal.

100470.q: Which of these metals is the least noble, that is, has the most negative standard potential?
100470.e: At about -3.04 V, lithium has one of the most negative standard potentials of all elements. It gives up its electrons particularly easily.
100470.m: Lithium is one of the least noble metals of all.

100471.q: What do you see when you dip a shiny iron nail into copper sulphate solution?
a: Copper is deposited on the nail
Iron is deposited on the nail
100471.e: Iron is less noble than copper and gives electrons to the copper ions. The iron dissolves and reddish-brown copper coats the nail.
100471.m: A less noble metal reduces the ions of a more noble metal.

100472.q: Which of these metals dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid, giving off hydrogen?
100472.e: Only metals with a negative standard potential can reduce oxonium ions to hydrogen. Magnesium is base, while copper, silver and gold are noble.
100472.m: Base metals dissolve in non-oxidising acids and form hydrogen.

100473.q: How can you recognise a noble metal in the electrochemical series?
100473.e: Noble metals have a higher standard potential than hydrogen, so a positive one. They give up electrons only with difficulty.
100473.m: Noble metals have a positive standard potential.

100474.q: Which of these metals has the highest standard potential?
100474.e: The redox pair Au³⁺/Au has a standard potential of about +1.5 V, higher than platinum, silver and copper. That is why gold is particularly resistant to corrosion.
100474.m: Among common metals, gold has the highest standard potential.

100475.q: Which element is the strongest oxidising agent in the electrochemical series?
100475.e: At about +2.87 V, the redox pair F₂/F⁻ has the highest standard potential. Fluorine therefore takes up electrons most strongly.
100475.m: Fluorine is the strongest elemental oxidising agent.

100476.q: What forms when chlorine water is added to a potassium bromide solution?
100476.e: Chlorine has a higher standard potential than bromine and oxidises bromide ions to bromine. The solution turns yellowish brown.
100476.m: A lighter halogen oxidises the ions of heavier halogens.

100477.q: What happens when you place a sheet of silver in copper sulphate solution?
100477.e: Silver is more noble than copper and cannot give electrons to copper ions. So no redox reaction takes place.
100477.m: A noble metal does not reduce the ions of a less noble metal.

100478.q: What does a strongly negative standard potential tell you about a metal?
a: It is a strong reducing agent
It is a strong oxidising agent
100478.e: A strongly negative standard potential means that the metal gives up its electrons very easily. This lets it reduce many other substances.
100478.m: The more negative the standard potential, the more strongly the metal reduces.

100479.q: Which ion concentration applies when measuring a standard electrode potential?
100479.e: Standard conditions include a concentration of 1 mol/L, 25 °C and about 1 bar pressure for gases. Other concentrations shift the potential.
100479.m: Standard potentials apply to concentrations of 1 mole per litre.

100480.q: Zinc has a standard potential of -0.76 V. What does this mean compared with the hydrogen electrode?
a: Zinc gives up electrons more easily than hydrogen
Zinc takes up electrons more easily than hydrogen
Zinc is more noble than hydrogen
100480.e: A negative standard potential marks a base metal. That is why zinc dissolves in hydrochloric acid, forming hydrogen.
100480.m: A negative standard potential marks a base metal.

100481.q: Copper has a standard potential of +0.34 V. What happens when you put copper in dilute hydrochloric acid?
100481.e: Copper is more noble than hydrogen and cannot reduce the oxonium ions of the acid. So no hydrogen forms and the copper stays intact.
100481.m: Metals with a positive standard potential are not attacked by dilute hydrochloric acid.

100482.q: What voltage does a cell made of magnesium (E° = -2.37 V) and silver (E° = +0.80 V) give under standard conditions?
100482.e: The cell voltage is E°(cathode) minus E°(anode). So 0.80 V minus (-2.37 V) = 3.17 V.
100482.m: The cell voltage is the difference between the two standard potentials.

100483.q: What voltage does a cell made of aluminium (E° = -1.66 V) and iron (E° = -0.44 V) give under standard conditions?
100483.e: Iron is more noble and forms the cathode. So -0.44 V minus (-1.66 V) = 1.22 V.
100483.m: A voltage also arises between two base metals.

100484.q: What material is the electrode of the standard hydrogen electrode made of?
100484.e: Platinum coated with finely divided platinum black catalyses the setting up of equilibrium between hydrogen gas and oxonium ions. It does not react itself.
100484.m: The hydrogen electrode needs a platinised platinum electrode.

100485.q: A galvanic cell has a positive cell voltage. What does this tell you about the reaction in the cell?
a: It constantly needs energy from outside
100485.e: A positive cell voltage corresponds to a negative Gibbs free energy of reaction. So the reaction supplies electrical energy by itself.
100485.m: A positive cell voltage shows a spontaneous reaction.

100486.q: Which chemist set up the equation for how electrode potentials depend on concentration in 1889?
100486.e: Walther Nernst formulated the equation named after him in 1889. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1920.
100486.m: The Nernst equation describes how the potential depends on concentration.

100487.q: At 25 °C, how does the potential of a half-cell with z = 1 change when the ion concentration falls to a tenth?
100487.e: At 25 °C, E = E° + (0.059 V/z)·lg(c). A tenth of the concentration means lg = -1, so a decrease of 0.059 V.
100487.m: With z equal to 1, the potential changes by about 59 millivolts per power of ten.

100488.q: What is the potential of a silver half-cell (E° = +0.80 V) at c(Ag⁺) = 0.01 mol/L and 25 °C?
100488.e: E = 0.80 V + 0.059 V·lg(0.01) = 0.80 V minus 0.118 V. This gives about +0.68 V.
100488.m: A lower ion concentration lowers the potential of a metal half-cell.

100489.q: At 25 °C, what voltage does a concentration cell made of two silver half-cells with 1 mol/L and 0.001 mol/L silver ions give?
100489.e: The difference in concentration is three powers of ten. With z = 1, ΔE = 3·0.059 V, so about 0.18 V.
100489.m: Even identical half-cells give a voltage if their concentrations differ.

100490.q: What is the potential of a hydrogen electrode at pH 7, 25 °C and 1 bar of hydrogen?
100490.e: For the hydrogen electrode, E = -0.059 V·pH. At pH 7 this gives about -0.41 V.
100490.m: The potential of the hydrogen electrode falls as the pH rises.

100491.q: Besides the gas constant R, which constant appears in the factor RT/(zF) of the Nernst equation?
100491.e: F is the Faraday constant, the charge of one mole of electrons. Together with R, T and z it forms the factor.
100491.m: The factor in the Nernst equation contains the gas constant, the temperature and the Faraday constant.

100492.q: What happens to the factor RT/(zF) when the temperature rises?
100492.e: The temperature T is in the numerator of the fraction. At a higher temperature, a change in concentration therefore has a bigger effect on the potential.
100492.m: At higher temperatures the potential depends more strongly on concentration.

100493.q: Which half-cell forms the anode in a concentration cell?
a: The one with the lower concentration
The one with the higher concentration
100493.e: The potential is lower in the dilute half-cell, so metal dissolves there. In this way the concentrations gradually even out.
100493.m: In a concentration cell, the dilute half-cell is oxidised.

100494.q: What is the potential of a nickel half-cell (E° = -0.25 V) at c(Ni²⁺) = 0.01 mol/L and 25 °C?
100494.m: For ions with a charge of two, the change in potential per power of ten is only half as large.

100495.q: Who received the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing the lithium-ion battery?
100495.e: John B. Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino were honoured in 2019. At 97, Goodenough was the oldest Nobel Prize winner up to then.
100495.m: The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry honoured the inventors of the lithium-ion battery.

100496.q: What material is the negative electrode of most lithium-ion batteries made of?
100496.e: Lithium ions can be stored between the layers of graphite during charging. Graphite is light, cheap and conducts well.
100496.m: The negative electrode of lithium-ion batteries is usually made of graphite.

100497.q: Which cathode material for lithium-ion batteries is considered particularly safe and needs no cobalt?
100497.e: Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) is very stable when heated and contains no cobalt. That is why it is increasingly used in electric cars and home storage systems.
100497.m: LFP batteries are particularly safe and need no cobalt.

100498.q: What is the nominal voltage of a typical lithium-ion cell with graphite and lithium cobalt oxide?
100498.e: The nominal voltage is typically 3.6 to 3.7 V. That is much more than nickel metal hydride or alkaline cells.
100498.m: A lithium-ion cell gives about 3.6 volts.

100499.q: Which company brought the first commercial lithium-ion battery onto the market in 1991?
100499.e: Sony sold the first lithium-ion batteries in 1991, at first for video cameras. This began their triumph in portable devices.
100499.m: Lithium-ion batteries have been on sale since 1991.

100500.q: What is the storing of lithium ions between the layers of graphite called?
100500.e: In intercalation, guest particles slip between the layers of a host lattice without destroying its structure. This lets lithium ions move back and forth during charging and discharging.
100500.m: During charging, lithium ions are intercalated into the graphite lattice.

100501.q: Why do lithium-ion batteries not contain a water-based electrolyte?
a: Water would break down at the high cell voltage
100501.e: The cell voltage is far above the decomposition voltage of water, and lithium also reacts with water. That is why lithium salts in organic solvents are used.
100501.m: Lithium-ion batteries need an organic, water-free electrolyte.

100502.q: What is the self-reinforcing overheating of a damaged lithium-ion cell called?
100502.e: In thermal runaway, breakdown reactions produce more and more heat. The cell can catch fire or burst.
100502.m: A damaged lithium battery can catch fire through thermal runaway.

100503.q: Where do the lithium ions move when you charge a lithium-ion battery?
a: From the positive electrode into the graphite
From the graphite to the positive electrode
They stay still in the electrolyte
They leave the battery as a gas
100503.e: During charging, lithium ions from the metal oxide of the positive electrode are stored between the layers of graphite. During discharging they move back again.
100503.m: During charging, lithium ions move into the graphite electrode.

100504.q: Which chemist teaching in Basel discovered the principle of the fuel cell in 1838?
100504.e: Christian Friedrich Schönbein, professor at the University of Basel, described the effect in 1838. William Grove built the first fuel cell shortly afterwards.
100504.m: The principle of the fuel cell was discovered in Basel in 1838.

100505.q: Which product forms in a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell?
100505.e: Hydrogen and oxygen react to form water. The reaction energy is used directly as electrical energy.
100505.m: A hydrogen fuel cell produces electricity, heat and water.

100506.q: Which particles pass through the membrane of a PEM fuel cell?
100506.e: PEM stands for proton exchange membrane. The membrane only lets protons through, so the electrons have to take the external circuit.
100506.m: Protons pass through the PEM membrane from the anode to the cathode.

100507.q: What is the theoretical cell voltage of a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell at 25 °C?
100507.e: The voltage is the difference between the standard potentials of oxygen and hydrogen. In practice, a cell under load usually gives only 0.6 to 0.9 V.
100507.m: A hydrogen fuel cell theoretically gives 1.23 volts.

100508.q: Which precious metal is usually used as a catalyst in PEM fuel cells?
100508.e: Platinum speeds up the splitting of hydrogen and the reduction of oxygen. Because it is expensive, researchers are working on catalysts with less platinum.
100508.m: PEM fuel cells usually need platinum as a catalyst.

100509.q: Which substance is oxidised at the anode of a hydrogen fuel cell?
100509.e: At the anode, hydrogen gives up electrons and forms protons. At the cathode, oxygen is reduced.
100509.m: In a fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode.

100510.q: Which type of fuel cell works with a ceramic electrolyte at temperatures above 600 °C?
100510.e: The SOFC uses an oxide ceramic that only conducts oxygen ions at high temperatures. In return, it can also use natural gas or biogas.
100510.m: Solid oxide fuel cells work at very high temperatures.

100511.q: Which type of fuel cell supplied electricity and drinking water on the Apollo moon missions?
100511.e: The Apollo spacecraft used alkaline fuel cells with potassium hydroxide solution as the electrolyte. The water produced served as drinking water for the crew.
100511.m: On the way to the Moon, alkaline fuel cells provided electricity and water.

100512.q: What fundamentally distinguishes a fuel cell from a battery?
100512.e: A battery contains its reactants from the start and eventually runs flat. A fuel cell supplies electricity as long as fuel and oxidising agent keep flowing in.
100512.m: A fuel cell works as long as fuel keeps being supplied.

a: A redox reaction forced by electric current
100513.e: In electrolysis, an external voltage forces a redox reaction that would not happen by itself. Electrical energy is converted into chemical energy.
100513.m: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to force a redox reaction.

100514.q: In which Swiss town did one of the first aluminium works in Europe start operating in 1888?
100514.e: The Aluminium-Industrie-Aktien-Gesellschaft (later Alusuisse) used the hydropower of the Rhine Falls in Neuhausen for molten salt electrolysis. Works in Valais were added later.
100514.m: The Swiss aluminium industry began at the Rhine Falls in 1888.

100515.q: Which three products does chlor-alkali electrolysis supply?
a: Chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide solution
100515.e: In the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution, chlorine forms at the anode and hydrogen at the cathode. Sodium hydroxide solution is left in the solution.
100515.m: Salt solution gives chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide solution.

100516.q: What is the voltage called that is needed in electrolysis on top of the theoretically calculated voltage?
100516.e: Because of hindrances at the electrodes, for example when gas forms, the calculated voltage is not enough. The overpotential depends strongly on the electrode material.
100516.m: Because of overpotential, electrolysis needs more voltage than calculated.

100517.q: What is the polarity of the cathode in electrolysis?
100517.e: In electrolysis, the cathode is connected to the negative terminal of the power source. Cations are reduced there.
100517.m: In electrolysis, the cathode is the negative terminal.

100518.q: In electrolytic copper refining, where do precious metals such as silver and gold collect?
100518.e: More noble metals are not oxidised at the anode and fall down as sludge. They are extracted profitably from this anode sludge.
100518.m: In copper refining, precious metals end up in the anode sludge.

100519.q: What is the electrolytic coating of an object with a layer of metal called?
100519.e: In electroplating, the object is the cathode, where metal ions from the solution are deposited. This is how parts are chrome-plated or gold-plated, for example.
100519.m: In electroplating, metal is deposited electrolytically on an object.

100520.q: Why is cryolite added in aluminium production?
100520.e: Pure aluminium oxide only melts at over 2000 °C. Dissolved in cryolite, molten salt electrolysis can take place at about 950 °C, which saves a lot of energy.
100520.m: Cryolite allows aluminium electrolysis at a lower temperature.

100521.q: Put simply, what is rust made of?
100521.e: Rust is a mixture of iron oxides and iron oxide hydroxides with varying water content. It is porous and does not protect the iron underneath.
100521.m: Rust is a porous layer of hydrated iron oxide.

100522.q: What is a short-circuited galvanic cell that causes corrosion on a metal surface called?
100522.e: When two different metals touch in the presence of an electrolyte, a local cell forms. The less noble metal dissolves.
100522.m: Local cells are tiny galvanic cells that destroy metal.

100523.q: Why do cars rust faster in winter on salted roads?
a: Salt lowers the temperature of the metal
100523.e: Dissolved road salt increases the electrical conductivity of water. This makes the electrochemical corrosion reactions run faster.
100523.m: Road salt speeds up corrosion because it makes water more conductive.

100524.q: What happens when a steel screw touches an aluminium sheet in damp conditions?
100524.e: Aluminium is less noble than iron and becomes the anode in contact corrosion. It therefore dissolves around the screw.
100524.m: In contact corrosion, the less noble metal dissolves.

100525.q: Why is aluminium resistant to corrosion in everyday life, even though it is a base metal?
a: It forms a dense oxide layer
It does not react with oxygen
100525.e: In air, aluminium immediately coats itself with a thin, dense layer of aluminium oxide. This passivation protects the metal underneath.
100525.m: A dense oxide layer passivates aluminium.

100526.q: Which alloying metal makes steel stainless?
100526.e: Above a certain chromium content, a thin, dense chromium oxide layer forms on the steel. It renews itself when scratched.
100526.m: Chromium protects stainless steel from rust with a dense oxide layer.

100527.q: What is the process called in which steel parts are dipped in molten zinc to protect them from corrosion?
100527.e: Hot-dip galvanising produces a firmly bonded zinc coating. Protected like this, crash barriers and masts last for decades.
100527.m: Hot-dip galvanised steel is protected from rust by a layer of zinc.

100528.q: Why does damaged tinplate rust especially fast at the scratch?
a: Tin is more noble than iron
Tin is less noble than iron
100528.e: Tinplate is tin-coated iron. If the tin layer is damaged, the less noble iron becomes the anode in the local cell and corrodes faster.
100528.m: A more noble protective layer only protects as long as it is undamaged.

100529.q: Which metal is suitable as a sacrificial anode for a steel ship's hull?
100529.e: A sacrificial anode must be less noble than the metal it protects. Zinc meets this condition, while copper, silver and lead are more noble than iron.
100529.m: Sacrificial anodes are made of a less noble metal than the protected part.

100530.q: Which household appliance often contains a magnesium sacrificial anode?
100530.e: Enamelled steel boilers are protected by a magnesium anode against corrosion at flaws in the enamel. It should be checked regularly.
100530.m: Many hot water boilers are protected by a magnesium anode.

100531.q: What is the protection principle called that the sacrificial anode belongs to?
100531.e: The protected metal is made the cathode, where no oxidation takes place. That is why it is called cathodic corrosion protection.
100531.m: A sacrificial anode makes the protected metal the cathode.

100532.q: Why does a sacrificial anode have to be replaced from time to time?
100532.e: The sacrificial anode is oxidised instead of the protected metal and dissolves. Once it is used up, the part itself starts to corrode.
100532.m: A sacrificial anode sacrifices itself and must therefore be renewed.

100533.q: What is cathodic protection called when a direct current source is used instead of a base metal?
100533.e: In impressed current protection, a power source pushes electrons into the part being protected. Pipelines and large steel structures are protected in this way, for example.
100533.m: In impressed current protection, a power source replaces the sacrificial anode.

100534.q: Which condition must be met between the sacrificial anode and the protected part?
a: They must be connected so that electricity can flow
They must be the same size
They must be made of the same metal
They must not be in the same water
100534.e: Electrons can only flow from the anode to the part through a conducting connection. Both must also be in the same electrolyte.
100534.m: The sacrificial anode and the part must be connected by a conductor.

100535.q: Why would copper be unsuitable as a sacrificial anode for an iron pipe?
a: Copper is more noble than iron
100535.e: Copper would become the cathode, and the iron would corrode even faster as the anode. A sacrificial anode must always be less noble.
100535.m: A more noble metal speeds up the corrosion of iron instead of preventing it.

100536.q: Where are sacrificial anodes typically fitted on ships?
a: On the hull below the waterline
100536.e: The steel needs protection where it is in the electrolyte, seawater. That is why the anodes are on the underwater part of the hull, often near the propeller too.
100536.m: Sacrificial anodes only work where they are in the water.

100537.q: At which university did Michael Grätzel develop the solar cell named after him?
100537.e: Michael Grätzel and Brian O'Regan presented the cell in 1991 at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne. It is a well-known Swiss invention.
100537.m: The Grätzel cell was invented at EPFL in Lausanne.

100538.q: What is the Grätzel cell also called?
100538.e: In the Grätzel cell, a dye absorbs the light and releases excited electrons. That is why it is called a dye-sensitised solar cell.
100538.m: The Grätzel cell is a dye-sensitised solar cell.

100539.q: Which nanoporous semiconductor takes up the electrons from the dye in the Grätzel cell?
100539.e: A porous layer of titanium dioxide nanoparticles offers a huge surface for the dye. It passes the electrons on to the electrode.
100539.m: In the Grätzel cell, titanium dioxide carries the electrons away.

100540.q: What happens to the dye in a Grätzel cell when light falls on it?
a: It is excited and releases an electron.
It takes up protons from the electrolyte.
It evaporates and has to be replaced.
It only turns the light into heat.
100540.e: The light lifts an electron in the dye to a higher energy level. This electron passes to the titanium dioxide and flows away as current.
100540.m: Light excites the dye to release an electron.

100541.q: Which natural process served as the model for the Grätzel cell?
100541.e: Like chlorophyll in plants, a dye captures the light. That is why it is also called artificial photosynthesis.
100541.m: The Grätzel cell copies the way plants collect light.

100542.q: What advantage does the Grätzel cell have over classic silicon cells?
a: It also works well in diffuse light
It has a much higher efficiency
100542.e: Grätzel cells also make good use of weak light and light falling at an angle, and they can be made coloured and translucent. However, their efficiency is usually lower.
100542.m: Grätzel cells also work in weak light.

100543.q: Thanks to their coloured, translucent design, what are Grätzel cells particularly suitable for?
a: as glass facades and windows on buildings
as a replacement for nuclear power stations
100543.e: Grätzel cells can be made coloured and partly transparent. The SwissTech Convention Center at EPFL in Lausanne has a facade made of such cells.
100543.m: Grätzel cells can be used as coloured glass facades.

100544.q: Why are Grätzel cells considered cheaper to make than classic solar cells?
a: They do not need high-purity silicon.
They are made almost entirely of gold.
100544.e: Silicon cells need extremely pure silicon, which takes a lot of energy to make. Grätzel cells use cheap substances such as titanium dioxide and are easier to manufacture.
100544.m: Grätzel cells do not need expensive ultra-pure silicon.

100545.q: Where is the energy stored in a redox flow cell?
100545.e: Two dissolved redox pairs are stored in separate tanks and pumped through the cell. So the energy is in the liquids.
100545.m: A redox flow battery stores energy in liquids.

100546.q: In the most common type of redox flow battery, which metal is dissolved in both electrolytes?
100546.e: The vanadium redox flow battery uses vanadium in different oxidation states. It is the most advanced type of flow battery.
100546.m: The best-known redox flow battery works with vanadium.

100547.q: Which special advantage characterises redox flow batteries?
a: Power and storage capacity can be scaled separately
They fit into any mobile phone
100547.e: The power depends on the size of the cell stack, the amount of energy on the size of the tanks. Both can be increased independently of each other.
100547.m: In flow batteries, the tanks determine the capacity and the cell stack the power.

100548.q: What separates the two electrolytes in the cell stack of a redox flow battery?
100548.e: The membrane stops the electrolytes from mixing but lets certain ions pass to balance the charge. It corresponds to the salt bridge of a galvanic cell.
100548.m: A membrane keeps the electrolytes of a flow battery apart.

100549.q: Why is it useful that both electrolytes of a vanadium flow battery contain the same element?
a: Crossing through the membrane does not ruin the electrolyte
It means no voltage is produced
100549.e: If ions pass through the membrane, only different oxidation states of the same element mix. The loss of capacity can then be fixed again by rebalancing.
100549.m: The same element on both sides makes the flow battery long-lasting.

100550.q: What are redox flow batteries mainly used for?
100550.e: Because of their low energy density, they are unsuitable for mobile devices. As large fixed storage systems, however, they can buffer electricity from sun and wind.
100550.m: Redox flow batteries are suitable as fixed grid storage.

100551.q: How do the electrolytes of a redox flow battery get into the cell stack?
a: They are filled in with spoons
They stay permanently in the stack
100551.e: Pumps move the electrolytes from the tanks past the electrodes and back. Running the pumps uses up part of the stored energy.
100551.m: Pumps keep the electrolytes of a flow battery moving.

100552.q: Why is vanadium particularly suitable for redox flow batteries?
a: It exists in several stable oxidation states
It is the lightest of all metals
It is the only metal that conducts electricity
100552.e: Vanadium can exist in solution in the oxidation states +2 to +5. This means both half-cells can run on the same element.
100552.m: Vanadium has several oxidation states and fills both sides of the flow battery.

100553.q: How long must a current of 5 A flow to transport 1 mol of electrons?
100553.e: t = Q/I = 96,485 C / 5 A ≈ 19,300 s. That is about 5.4 hours.
100553.m: The time is the charge divided by the current.

100554.q: How much copper (M = 63.55 g/mol) is deposited when a current of 2 A flows through copper sulphate solution for 1 hour?
100554.m: More current and more time deposit more copper.

100555.q: How much silver (M = 107.9 g/mol) does a current of 1 A deposit in 965 seconds?
100555.e: Q = 1 A · 965 s = 965 C, which is 0.01 mol of electrons. Silver ions have a charge of one, so 0.01 mol · 107.9 g/mol ≈ 1.08 g forms.
100555.m: A hundredth of a mole of electrons deposits a hundredth of a mole of silver.

100556.q: What does Faraday's second law state?
a: The same charge deposits amounts of substance in the ratio 1/z
The voltage is proportional to time
Gases only form at the anode
The mass does not depend on the charge
100556.e: If the same charge flows through different electrolytes, the deposited masses are in the ratio of their molar masses divided by the ion charge z. These are called equivalent masses.
100556.m: Equal charges deposit chemically equivalent amounts of substance.

100557.q: In which decade did Michael Faraday publish his laws of electrolysis?
100557.e: Faraday formulated the laws in 1833 and 1834. Terms such as electrode, anode, cathode and ion also come from him.
100557.m: Faraday laid the foundations of electrolysis in the 1830s.

100558.q: What charge is needed to deposit 1 mol of aluminium from Al³⁺ ions?
100558.e: Each aluminium ion needs three electrons. So Q = 3 · 96,485 C ≈ 289,500 C.
100558.m: Ions with a charge of three need three times the Faraday charge per mole.

100559.q: What charge is needed to produce 1 mol of hydrogen gas (H₂) by electrolysis?
100559.e: For one H₂ molecule, two protons are each reduced with one electron. So Q = 2 · 96,485 C ≈ 193,000 C.
100559.m: One mole of hydrogen gas needs two moles of electrons.

100560.q: What does Faraday's first law state?
a: The deposited mass is proportional to the charge
The voltage is proportional to the mass
The mass depends only on the temperature
100560.e: The amount of substance deposited is proportional to the charge that has flowed, Q = I · t. Double the charge deposits double the mass.
100560.m: The deposited mass grows in proportion to the charge that has flowed.

100561.q: What innovation did Abraham Darby introduce in iron smelting at Coalbrookdale in 1709?
a: Coke instead of charcoal as fuel
Electricity instead of fire in the blast furnace
100561.e: Coke made from coal replaced the increasingly scarce charcoal. This meant iron could be produced in much larger quantities and more cheaply.
100561.m: With coke, iron became the mass material of industrialisation.

100562.q: Which structure of 1779 in the English county of Shropshire is regarded as the first large cast-iron bridge?
100562.e: The Iron Bridge spans the Severn near Coalbrookdale. It showed that iron was also suitable as a building material for large structures.
100562.m: The Iron Bridge is a landmark of the Industrial Revolution.

100563.q: Who published the book “The Condition of the Working Class in England” in 1845?
100563.e: In it, Engels described the living and working conditions of factory workers in Manchester. The work is regarded as an early piece of social reporting on industrialisation.
100563.m: Friedrich Engels described the misery of English factory workers.

100564.q: In the 19th century, what were the problems of the working class, such as poverty, housing shortages and child labour, called?
100564.e: With industrialisation, cities grew quickly, and many working families lived in great hardship. Trade unions, churches, employers and the state looked for solutions.
100564.m: The social question was the great problem of the industrial age.

100565.q: Which rules did the Swiss federal Factory Act of 1877 introduce, among others?
a: The eleven-hour day and a ban on factory work under 14
The 40-hour week and four weeks' holiday
A ban on all steam engines in towns
100565.e: The law limited daily working time to eleven hours and banned factory work for children under 14. Federal factory inspectors checked that it was obeyed.
100565.m: The Factory Act of 1877 was a milestone in worker protection in Switzerland.

100566.q: Which railway line opened in 1830 as the first intercity railway run to a timetable using only steam locomotives?
100566.e: On the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, passenger and goods trains ran to a timetable. At the Rainhill Trials in 1829, Stephenson's “Rocket” had won out as the locomotive.
100566.m: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened the age of intercity railways in 1830.

100567.q: Which branch of industry is regarded as the first leading sector of industrialisation in Great Britain?
100567.e: Cotton processing was the first to be mechanised on a large scale. It pulled mechanical engineering, coal and iron along with it.
100567.m: The cotton industry stood at the start of industrialisation.

100568.q: Which energy source mainly powered the early Swiss factories, since the country had hardly any coal of its own?
100568.e: Spinning and weaving mills were therefore often built on rivers such as the Töss, Aabach or Linth. Waterwheels and later turbines supplied the power.
100568.m: Swiss industrialisation first ran on water power.

100569.q: Which cantonal government issued an ordinance in 1815 banning factory work for children under nine?
100569.e: The Zurich ordinance of 1815 is regarded as one of the earliest child protection laws in Europe. It mainly concerned the new cotton spinning mills.
100569.m: Zurich protected young children from factory work as early as 1815.

100570.q: What is the spinning machine called that James Hargreaves invented around 1764, which drove several spindles by hand?
100570.e: With the Spinning Jenny, one person could spin many threads at once. The yarn, however, was still relatively weak.
100570.m: The Spinning Jenny multiplied the work of the spinning wheel.

100571.q: Who patented the water-powered spinning machine “Water Frame” in 1769?
100571.e: The Water Frame produced strong yarn that was suitable as warp thread. Because it ran on water power, it needed large factory buildings by rivers.
100571.m: Arkwright's Water Frame brought spinning into the factory.

100572.q: Which spinning machine by Samuel Crompton (1779) combined the advantages of the Spinning Jenny and the Water Frame?
100572.e: A “mule” is a cross between two animals, just like the machine itself. It produced yarn that was fine and strong at the same time.
100572.m: The Spinning Mule combined two earlier spinning machines.

100573.q: What is the water-powered spinning mill that Richard Arkwright opened in Cromford in 1771 regarded as?
a: One of the first modern factories
100573.e: In Cromford, hundreds of people worked at machines in shifts at fixed times. The site is now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
100573.m: Cromford is regarded as the cradle of the factory system.

100574.q: What energy drove the first mechanical cotton spinning mills in Switzerland, such as the Hard spinning mill on the Töss?
100574.e: The Hard spinning mill in Wülflingen started operating in 1802. Like many early factories, it stood on a river and used waterwheels for power.
100574.m: Early Swiss spinning mills stood on rivers and used water power.

100575.q: Which spinning method, developed in the USA in the 19th century, is still the most widespread in the world today?
100575.e: On a ring spinning machine, a small traveller runs on a ring around the spindle and twists the thread. The method works continuously and produces very even yarn.
100575.m: Ring spinning is the most important spinning method today.

100576.q: Which Winterthur company is one of the world's leading makers of spinning machinery?
100576.e: Rieter was founded in 1795 and makes machines and systems for producing yarn. Schindler, by contrast, builds lifts, and Stadler builds rail vehicles.
100576.m: Rieter from Winterthur builds spinning machinery for the whole world.

100577.q: How was cotton spinning mainly organised in the Zurich Oberland before mechanisation?
a: As home work in the putting-out system
In the guilds of the towns
100577.e: Merchants delivered raw cotton to families who spun at home, and then collected the yarn. The spinning machines soon made this home work unprofitable.
100577.m: Before spinning machines, people spun at home in many living rooms.

100578.q: Who patented a mechanical, power-driven loom in 1785?
100578.e: Edmund Cartwright was actually a clergyman. His power loom was improved over the following decades until it replaced hand weaving.
100578.m: Edmund Cartwright invented the power loom.

100579.q: Which invention by John Kay (1733) greatly sped up weaving and made the shortage of yarn worse?
100579.e: With the flying shuttle, the weaver shot the shuttle through the shed using a cord. Because weavers now worked faster, hand-spun yarn was no longer enough.
100579.m: The flying shuttle made weaving faster than spinning.

100580.q: What happened in the “Uster fire” in November 1832?
a: Home weavers set fire to a mechanical weaving mill
100580.e: Angry hand weavers set fire to the Corrodi & Pfister weaving mill in Oberuster. They feared the weaving machines would take away their income.
100580.m: The Uster fire was the best-known machine-breaking incident in Switzerland.

100581.q: Which play by Gerhart Hauptmann deals with the uprising of Silesian weavers in 1844?
100581.e: “The Weavers” was published in 1892 and shows the hardship of the home weavers. “The Robbers” is by Schiller, “The Physicists” by Dürrenmatt.
100581.m: Hauptmann's play “The Weavers” recalls the weavers' uprising of 1844.

100582.q: What were the English textile workers called who destroyed textile machines in protest from 1811?
100582.e: The Luddites claimed to follow a legendary leader called Ned Ludd. Even today, opponents of technology are sometimes called “Luddites”.
100582.m: The Luddites fought the new machines with violence.

100583.q: In weaving, what are the threads called that are inserted across the warp?
100583.e: The warp threads run lengthways and are stretched on the loom. The weft thread is passed across them and so interlaced with them.
100583.m: Fabric is made of warp and weft.

100584.q: What do modern air-jet, rapier and projectile weaving machines have in common?
a: They weave without the classic shuttle
They are controlled by punched cards
100584.e: These shuttleless weaving machines insert the weft thread using compressed air, rapiers or small projectiles. This makes them much faster than looms with shuttles.
100584.m: Modern weaving machines manage without a shuttle.

100585.q: Which innovation of the Northrop loom from the 1890s allowed one person to look after many looms?
a: Automatic changing of the weft bobbin
100585.e: When the thread in the shuttle ran out, the machine inserted a new bobbin by itself. So the loom no longer had to be stopped for each change.
100585.m: The Northrop loom changed its bobbins by itself.

100586.q: At which trade fair was the term “Industry 4.0” presented to a wide public in 2011?
100586.e: Experts from science and industry presented the concept in Hanover in 2011. It then became a future project of the German federal government.
100586.m: Industry 4.0 became known at the Hannover Messe in 2011.

100587.q: What are systems called in which mechanical components are connected to the internet via sensors and software?
100587.e: Cyber-physical systems link real machines with digital data processing. They are the technical basis of Industry 4.0.
100587.m: In cyber-physical systems, machine and software merge.

100588.q: What is a virtual copy of a real machine, fed with its real-time data, called?
100588.e: With a digital twin, operation, wear and changes can be simulated on the computer. In this way faults can be detected before they occur on the real equipment.
100588.m: A digital twin recreates a machine in the computer.

100589.q: What is maintenance called that uses sensor data to predict an impending failure?
100589.e: Sensors measure things such as vibration or temperature, and algorithms detect patterns before a fault. Parts are thus replaced only shortly before they would fail.
100589.m: Predictive maintenance repairs before something breaks.

100590.q: What does the goal “batch size 1” mean in Industry 4.0?
a: Making one-off items as economically as mass-produced goods
Making only one product per factory
Setting up only one machine per hall
100590.e: Networked, flexible equipment is meant to make individually customised products at costs similar to those of series products. This is also called mass customisation.
100590.m: Batch size 1 means individual production at series costs.

100591.q: Which vendor-independent communication standard is often used for data exchange between industrial machines?
100591.e: OPC UA (Open Platform Communications Unified Architecture) describes data together with their meaning. This allows machines from different manufacturers to work together.
100591.m: OPC UA is a common language for industrial machines.

100592.q: What are robots called that work directly with people without a safety fence?
100592.e: Cobots have force and touch sensors and stop immediately on contact. They take over heavy or monotonous parts of tasks alongside people.
100592.m: Cobots work hand in hand with people.

100593.q: What is the networking of machines, sensors and workpieces over the internet in industry called in English?
100593.e: In the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), devices constantly report their status to other systems. This creates self-organising production.
100593.m: The Industrial Internet of Things connects machines over the network.

100594.q: Which generation of mobile communications is regarded as important for wirelessly networked factories because of its very short delay times?
100594.e: 5G offers low latency and can connect many devices at the same time. Some companies run their own 5G campus networks for this.
100594.m: 5G enables fast wireless connections in the factory.

100595.q: Roughly how much did the moving assembly line shorten the assembly time of a Ford Model T?
a: From about 1 day to about 20 hours
100595.e: Before, assembling a car took about twelve and a half hours. With the moving line it fell to about 93 minutes.
100595.m: The assembly line made car assembly many times faster.

100596.q: Which businesses in Chicago inspired Ford's engineers to use assembly line work?
100596.e: In the slaughterhouses, carcasses hung on moving hooks and were cut up station by station. Ford reversed this principle and put cars together step by step.
100596.m: The assembly line was copied from the disassembly lines of the slaughterhouses.

100597.q: Why did Ford introduce the “five-dollar day” in 1914?
a: To lower the high rate at which workers quit
Because the state required a minimum wage
To be able to sell the cars at a higher price
Because the unions won a strike
100597.e: The monotonous work on the line led to a great many resignations. The roughly doubled daily wage tied the workers to Ford and at the same time made them possible car buyers.
100597.m: The five-dollar day was meant to keep workers on the assembly line.

100598.q: Roughly how many Ford Model Ts were built from 1908 to 1927?
100598.e: Mass production lowered the price so much that many families could afford a car. The Model T long remained the most-built car in the world.
100598.m: The Model T was built about 15 million times.

100599.q: What was new about Ford's assembly line from 1913 compared with earlier assembly lines with fixed work stations?
a: The car was brought to the workers on a moving belt
The workers built each car alone from start to finish
The cars were assembled by robots for the first time
The parts were made of wood for the first time
100599.e: There had already been assembly lines with fixed stations, for example at Ransom Olds. Ford added the moving line, which set the pace.
100599.m: Ford's innovation was the moving assembly line.

100600.q: What is the economic model called that combines mass production on the assembly line with mass consumption through higher wages?
100600.e: The term goes back to Henry Ford. Standardised products, large quantities and workers with purchasing power shaped industry until the 1970s.
100600.m: Fordism combines mass production and mass consumption.

100601.q: Which film by Charlie Chaplin (1936) criticises monotonous work on the assembly line?
100601.e: In “Modern Times”, Chaplin's character literally gets caught up in the gears of a machine. The film shows how the line sets the pace for people.
100601.m: Chaplin's “Modern Times” shows people as cogs in the machine.

100602.q: What is the time available at each station of an assembly line for one work step called?
100602.e: All stations work at the same pace so that the line keeps moving evenly. The work is divided so that each step fits into the cycle time.
100602.m: On the assembly line, the cycle time sets the working pace.

100603.q: Which car was the first to be made on an assembly line in Germany, from 1924?
100603.e: Because of its green colour, the Opel 4 PS was popularly called the “Laubfrosch” (tree frog). Opel adopted American production methods for it.
100603.m: The Opel Laubfrosch was the first German assembly line car.

100604.q: Who founded the firm Escher Wyss in Zurich in 1805?
a: Hans Caspar Escher and Salomon von Wyss
Alfred Escher and Johann Jakob Sulzer
Hans Konrad Escher von der Linth and Johann Rieter
100604.e: Hans Caspar Escher contributed the technical knowledge, the banker Salomon von Wyss the capital. The company name is made up of both family names.
100604.m: Escher Wyss bears the names of its two founders.

100605.q: What did Escher Wyss start with in 1805?
100605.e: The firm started as a cotton spinning mill in the Neumühle in Zurich. Because the machines had to be built and repaired in-house, a machine workshop soon developed.
100605.m: Escher Wyss was first a spinning mill.

100606.q: Which vehicles did Escher Wyss build from 1835, becoming known on many lakes?
100606.e: Escher Wyss built ships together with their boilers and steam engines. Many paddle steamers on Swiss and foreign lakes come from Zurich.
100606.m: Escher Wyss built steamships for many lakes.

100607.q: Why did Escher Wyss close its spinning mill in 1860?
a: Mechanical engineering had become more important
100607.e: Building machines, turbines and ships had overtaken spinning economically. Escher Wyss thus became entirely an engineering company.
100607.m: The Escher Wyss spinning mill turned into a machine factory.

100608.q: Which company took over Escher Wyss in 1969?
100608.e: After a fall in sales, Escher Wyss passed entirely to Sulzer in Winterthur. In 1983 this became Sulzer-Escher Wyss AG.
100608.m: From 1969 Escher Wyss belonged to Sulzer.

100609.q: Besides steamships, what did Escher Wyss build in the 19th century that made the Zurich firm known abroad too?
100609.e: Escher Wyss developed from a spinning mill into a machine factory. Turbines and machines from Zurich were delivered to many countries, soon also from works abroad.
100609.m: In the 19th century Escher Wyss was known for turbines and machines.

100610.q: In which field was Escher Wyss a world leader in the 20th century?
100610.e: Escher Wyss supplied water turbines and other hydraulic equipment to many countries. The firm also built steam turbines and refrigeration plants.
100610.m: Escher Wyss was a specialist in water turbines.

100611.q: Which place in Zurich's industrial district still recalls the company in its name today?
100611.e: The Escher Wyss site lay in District 5 on the Limmat. After industry ended, the district became a residential and nightlife area.
100611.m: Escher-Wyss-Platz recalls the Zurich machine factory.

100612.q: What did Sulzer start with in Winterthur in 1834?
100612.e: Johann Jakob Sulzer and his sons built an iron foundry outside the town walls. Before that the family had run a turning shop and brass foundry.
100612.m: Sulzer began as an iron foundry in Winterthur.

100613.q: Under which name was the company Sulzer, founded in Winterthur in 1834, run for a long time?
100613.e: Johann Jakob Sulzer founded the foundry together with his sons, who ran the business. The name “Gebrüder Sulzer” became a world-famous brand.
100613.m: Sulzer was long called Gebrüder Sulzer.

100614.q: With which machines did Sulzer have great international success in the 1880s?
100614.e: Sulzer built powerful steam engines for factories and power stations and exported them to many countries. As a result, the number of employees rose sharply.
100614.m: In the 19th century Sulzer became internationally known for steam engines.

100615.q: Which type of engine made Sulzer world-famous in the 20th century, above all in shipbuilding?
100615.e: For decades, Sulzer marine diesels powered many large merchant ships. The slow-running two-stroke engines are especially economical.
100615.m: Sulzer was famous for large marine diesel engines.

100616.q: Which Sulzer weaving machine became an export success from the 1950s?
100616.e: In this machine, a small metal projectile carries the weft thread through the shed. It was faster and quieter than looms with shuttles and became an export success.
100616.m: Sulzer revolutionised weaving with the projectile weaving machine.

100617.q: Why did Swiss industrial firms such as Sulzer open works abroad in the 19th century, for example in Ludwigshafen in 1881?
a: To avoid customs duties and produce closer to customers
Because factories were banned in Switzerland
Because there were no workers in Switzerland
Because machines were not allowed to cross borders
100617.e: With a works in Germany, Sulzer could supply the large German market directly without paying high import duties. Around 1900 the company already employed about 3000 people.
100617.m: With works abroad, Swiss firms opened up large markets.

100618.q: Under which name is the large engine business from the Sulzer tradition continued in Winterthur today?
100618.e: Sulzer sold the diesel engine business to Wärtsilä in 1997. In 2015 this gave rise to the independent company WinGD, which develops marine engines.
100618.m: Sulzer's marine engines live on in WinGD.

100619.q: Which product does Sulzer mainly focus on today (as of 2025)?
100619.e: Sulzer has changed from a broad engineering group into a specialist in pumps, separation technology and service. Its headquarters are still in Winterthur.
100619.m: Today Sulzer is known above all for pumps.

100620.q: When and where was the firm Brown, Boveri & Cie. founded?
100620.e: The firm was founded in 1891 in Baden in the canton of Aargau. As a result, the town grew into an important industrial centre.
100620.m: BBC was founded in Baden in 1891.

100621.q: How did Charles Brown and Walter Boveri divide the tasks when founding BBC?
a: Brown was the engineer, Boveri the businessman
Brown was a banker, Boveri a chemist
Brown was a politician, Boveri an architect
100621.e: The engineer Charles E. L. Brown designed generators and motors. Walter Boveri took care of organisation, financing and sales.
100621.m: At BBC, technical skill and business sense complemented each other.

100622.q: With which Swedish company did BBC merge in 1988 to form ABB?
100622.e: ASEA and Brown Boveri became Asea Brown Boveri, ABB for short. Each partner held 50 per cent, and the headquarters were set up in Zurich.
100622.m: BBC and ASEA formed ABB in 1988.

100623.q: Which machines did BBC build from 1901, together with turbo generators, as its main business?
100623.e: A steam turbine and a generator together form a turbo set for power stations. Such plants became BBC's most important business.
100623.m: BBC grew big with turbines and generators for power stations.

100624.q: Which component, based on an invention by the Swiss Alfred Büchi, did BBC make from the 1920s?
100624.e: A turbocharger uses the energy of the exhaust gases to force more air into the engine. This greatly increases the power of diesel and marine engines.
100624.m: BBC built turbochargers based on Alfred Büchi's principle.

100625.q: What position did BBC hold in the Swiss economy around 1910?
a: Largest company in Swiss mechanical engineering
100625.e: Less than 20 years after it was founded, BBC had overtaken all the country's other engineering firms. The reason was the boom in electrification.
100625.m: Around 1910 BBC was the largest Swiss engineering firm.

100626.q: With which Zurich machine factory did BBC merge in 1967?
100626.e: MFO was a long-established maker of electrical machines. In 1969 BBC also took over Sécheron in Geneva.

100627.q: Why did BBC set up a large subsidiary in Germany as early as 1900?
a: To supply the large German market directly
Because industry was banned in Switzerland
Because there was no electricity in Switzerland
100627.e: The subsidiary in Mannheim supplied the large German market locally. It grew so much that from about 1930 it was bigger than the parent company in Baden.
100627.m: BBC grew early through a large subsidiary in Germany.

100628.q: Who brought the knowledge of watchmaking to Geneva from around 1550?
100628.e: Protestant refugees from France settled in Reformed Geneva. There their watchmaking skills combined with the craft of gold and silversmiths.

100629.q: How did the strict Geneva dress codes under Calvin affect crafts?
a: All craftsmen had to become farmers
100629.e: Showy jewellery was frowned upon, whereas a watch was regarded as a useful object. So many goldsmiths switched to cases and watches.
100629.m: Calvin's ban on jewellery indirectly promoted Geneva watchmaking.

100630.q: Which circumstance favoured watchmaking in the Neuchâtel mountains from the 17th century?
a: There were rich gold mines there
There was a particularly warm climate there
100630.e: Without guild restrictions, anyone could freely take up a trade. Many farming families made watch parts at home in winter.
100630.m: Without guild rules, watchmaking flourished in the Neuchâtel Jura.

100631.q: Roughly what share of the watches made worldwide did Switzerland produce around 1870?
100631.e: Around 1870 Switzerland was clearly the leader in the world watch market. Soon afterwards, however, competition from the USA with machine production grew.
100631.m: Around 1870 about 70 per cent of the world's watches came from Switzerland.

100632.q: By how much did the number of people employed in the Swiss watch industry fall as a result of the quartz crisis?
100632.e: At the end of the 1960s about 90,000 people worked in the industry, by the mid-1980s only about 30,000. Cheap quartz watches from Asia pushed out many mechanical watches.
100632.m: The quartz crisis cost the watch industry more than half its jobs.

100633.q: Which Japanese company put the first quartz wristwatch on sale in 1969?
100633.e: The Seiko Astron came onto the market at the end of 1969. It was much more accurate than mechanical watches and began the quartz crisis.
100633.m: The Seiko Astron was the first quartz wristwatch you could buy.

100634.q: Where were the first Swiss prototypes of a quartz wristwatch made?
a: At the Centre électronique horloger in Neuchâtel
100634.e: The Swiss watch industry's laboratory in Neuchâtel presented the first prototypes in 1967, which led to the Beta 21 quartz movement. At first, however, Switzerland hardly made use of this lead.
100634.m: Switzerland built quartz watches early but relied on mechanics for a long time.

100635.q: Which two towns in the canton of Neuchâtel became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2009 for their “watchmaking town planning”?
100635.e: Both towns were rebuilt on a grid pattern after fires. The houses have large windows so that the watchmakers had plenty of daylight.
100635.m: La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle are World Heritage Sites of the watch industry.

100636.q: Which entrepreneur led the struggling Swiss watch industry back to success with the Swatch Group from the 1980s?
100636.e: Hayek led the groups ASUAG and SSIH, merged in 1983, and backed the cheap plastic Swatch. Hans Wilsdorf founded Rolex, and Alfred Escher shaped railways and banks.
100636.m: Nicolas G. Hayek made the Swatch Group big.

100637.q: What was the profession of Pierre Jaquet-Droz, who built the famous automata with his son?
100637.e: Pierre Jaquet-Droz was a watchmaker from La Chaux-de-Fonds. With his son Henri-Louis and the mechanic Jean-Frédéric Leschot, he created three human-like automata between 1768 and 1774.
100637.m: The automata were made by a family of watchmakers.

100638.q: Which three figures make up the Jaquet-Droz automata?
a: The Writer, the Draughtsman and the Musician
The Cook, the Gardener and the Dancer
The Smith, the Baker and the Weaver
The Drummer, the Flautist and the Singer
100638.e: Each figure carries out its own activity with the help of cam discs and levers. The automata still work today.
100638.m: The Writer, the Draughtsman and the Musician form the Jaquet-Droz trio.

100639.q: Roughly how many parts does the Writer consist of?
100639.e: The Writer is the most complex of the three automata. The Draughtsman and the Musician each consist of about 2000 to 2500 parts.
100639.m: The Writer contains about 6000 individual parts.

100640.q: Why is the Writer regarded as an early forerunner of the programmable computer?
a: Its text can be set freely using a wheel with interchangeable characters
It stores data on magnetic tape
It is controlled by a keyboard
100640.e: Using a disc with interchangeable cams, you can set any text of up to 40 characters. The machine then carries out this “program” on its own.
100640.m: The Writer is a mechanically programmable automaton.

100641.q: Which king does the Draughtsman of the Jaquet-Droz automata portray?
100641.e: The Draughtsman can make four pictures, including a portrait of Louis XV and a dog with the caption “Mon toutou”. In between he blows the dust off his pencil.
100641.m: The Draughtsman can draw a portrait of Louis XV.

100642.q: What is special about the Musician of the Jaquet-Droz automata?
a: She plays a real organ with her fingers
She sings with a real voice
100642.e: The Musician really presses the keys of a specially built organ with her fingers. Her head and eyes move, and her chest rises as if she were breathing.
100642.m: The Musician plays a real organ herself.

100643.q: In which museum are the Jaquet-Droz automata displayed today?
a: In the Musée d'art et d'histoire in Neuchâtel
In the National Museum in Zurich
In the Swiss Museum of Transport in Lucerne
100643.e: The automata returned to Switzerland from abroad at the beginning of the 20th century. They are regularly demonstrated in the Museum of Art and History in Neuchâtel.
100643.m: The Jaquet-Droz automata are in Neuchâtel.

100644.q: What did the automata mainly serve their builders for in the 18th century?
a: As advertising for their watches at royal courts
100644.e: The Jaquet-Droz family showed the figures at European courts and so made their skill known. This brought them wealthy customers for watches and music boxes.
100644.m: The automata advertised the Jaquet-Droz watches.

100645.q: What is the title of Frederick Winslow Taylor's main work, published in 1911?
a: The Theory of the Leisure Class
100645.e: In it Taylor described how work could be made more efficient using scientific methods. The book founded “scientific management”.
100645.m: Taylor's main work is called The Principles of Scientific Management.

100646.q: Which principle is typical of Taylorism?
a: Separating planning work from the work of carrying it out
100646.e: Management plans every task precisely, and the workers only carry it out. To do this, the work is broken down into small, simple steps.
100646.m: In Taylorism, brain work is separated from manual work.

100647.q: With what tool did Taylor study the individual work steps?
a: With a stopwatch in time studies
100647.e: Taylor measured how long each part of a movement took. From this he set the best way of working and a standard output.
100647.m: Time studies with a stopwatch are the tool of Taylorism.

100648.q: At which steelworks did Taylor carry out his well-known experiments on loading pig iron?
100648.e: At Bethlehem Steel, Taylor increased a worker's loading output with precise instructions for movements and breaks. He also optimised shovel sizes there.
100648.m: Taylor's pig iron experiments took place at Bethlehem Steel.

100649.q: Which form of pay did Taylor propose to spur workers to higher output?
a: Performance pay with a bonus for meeting the quota
A fixed monthly wage for everyone
100649.e: Anyone who reached the set daily quota received a much higher piece rate. Anyone who fell short received less.
100649.m: Taylor relied on performance pay as an incentive.

100650.q: Which married couple added precise motion studies to Taylor's time studies?
100650.e: The Gilbreths broke work processes down into basic movements and filmed them. The aim was to cut out unnecessary movements.
100650.m: The Gilbreths studied every hand movement at work.

100651.q: Which German association was founded in 1924 to standardise time studies and work design?
100651.e: REFA originally stood for the Reich Committee for Working Time Determination. REFA methods for timing work are still taught today.
100651.m: REFA brought Taylor's ideas into German companies.

100652.q: Which criticism is often made of Taylorism?
a: Monotonous work and loss of skills
Too much say for the workers
Training periods that are too long
100652.e: Anyone who only repeats one small movement needs hardly any skill and often finds the work meaningless. Later ideas such as group work were meant to counter this.
100652.m: Taylorism increases output but often makes work dull.

100653.q: Which three conditions must an invention meet to get a patent?
a: Novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability
Beauty, size and a high price
100653.e: The invention must not already be publicly known and must not be obvious to experts. It must also be possible to make or use it in trade or industry.
100653.m: Patents are only granted for new, inventive and applicable solutions.

100654.q: What is the maximum length of time a patent can be valid in Switzerland?
100654.e: The patent must be kept in force by paying fees every year and ends 20 years after filing at the latest. After that, anyone may use the invention.
100654.m: A patent protects an invention for no more than 20 years.

100655.q: Which federal authority grants patents in Switzerland?
a: The Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property
The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority
100655.e: The IPI in Bern is responsible for patents, trade marks and designs. Many companies also file their inventions with the European Patent Office.
100655.m: The IPI in Bern is the Swiss patent office.

100656.q: Which famous physicist worked at the patent office in Bern from 1902 to 1909?
100656.e: Einstein examined patent applications there as a technical expert. During this time, in 1905, he also published the special theory of relativity.
100656.m: Einstein was an expert at the Bern patent office.

100657.q: In which year did the first Swiss federal patent law come into force?
100657.e: For a long time Switzerland had no patent law, which led to accusations of copying. After a constitutional amendment in 1887, the Federal Act on Invention Patents followed in 1888.
100657.m: Switzerland has had a patent law since 1888.

100658.q: Which city republic passed one of the world's first patent laws in 1474?
100658.e: The Venetian law protected new, useful inventions from copying for ten years. It already contained the main features of modern patent law.
100658.m: Venice protected inventions by law as early as 1474.

100659.q: What must an inventor do in return for patent protection?
a: Give the invention to the state
100659.e: The patent specification is published so that everyone can learn from the idea. In return, the inventor receives an exclusive right for a limited time.
100659.m: A patent trades disclosure for protection for a limited time.

100660.q: Which of these countries files the most patents with the European Patent Office relative to its population (as of 2024)?
100660.e: Measured by population, Switzerland has topped the European Patent Office's patent statistics for years. This shows the strong research in industry and universities.
100660.m: Per head, Switzerland is the European champion of patent filings.

100661.q: In which kind of area do especially many cacti grow?
a: In the ice at the North Pole
100661.e: Cacti are adapted to great drought. That is why many of them are found in deserts and semi-deserts.

100662.q: What are a cactus's spines for?
100662.e: The sharp spines stop thirsty animals from nibbling the cactus. They also give a little shade.
100662.m: Spines protect the cactus from hungry animals.

100663.q: What does the giant saguaro cactus in the desert look like?
a: Like a star on the ground
100663.e: The saguaro can grow over 12 metres tall. With its arms it looks like a big candlestick.
100663.m: The saguaro is a giant among cacti.

100664.q: What do many cacti show only for a short time?
100664.e: Many cacti produce splendid, colourful flowers. Some flowers last only a single day or night.
100664.m: Even a spiny cactus can flower beautifully.

100665.q: How often does a cactus on the windowsill need water?
100665.e: A cactus stores water and cannot cope with waterlogging. Too much watering makes its roots rot.
100665.m: A cactus is watered only rarely.

100666.q: Why must you peel the fruit of the prickly pear carefully?
100666.e: The prickly pear cactus produces sweet fruits. Their skin has fine spines, so they are peeled carefully.

100667.q: Where do the leaves grow on a palm tree?
100667.e: Most palms have a trunk without branches. The big leaves form a tuft at the top.
100667.m: Palms wear their leaves like a hat on top.

100668.q: Which sweet fruits grow on palms in the desert?
100668.e: The date palm grows in desert oases. Its sweet fruits are dates.
100668.m: Dates grow on the date palm.

100669.q: In which Swiss canton do you see especially many palms outdoors?
100669.e: The climate in Ticino is mild. There, for example, windmill palms even grow wild in the woods.

100670.q: Which hard fruit with juice inside grows on a palm?
100670.e: The coconut grows on the coconut palm. Inside it has white flesh and coconut water.
100670.m: The coconut grows on the coconut palm.

100671.q: What weather do most palms like?
100671.e: Most palms grow in the tropics and subtropics. Only a few kinds can cope with frost.

100672.q: From the stems of which plants is rattan furniture made?
100672.e: Rattan comes from climbing palms in Asia. Their long, flexible stems are woven into chairs and baskets.

100673.q: How tall can some palms grow?
a: Only as tall as a child
Only as tall as a table
Only as tall as a blade of grass
100673.e: The tallest palm is the wax palm in Colombia. It can grow about 60 metres tall, as tall as a tower block.

100674.q: What is a bamboo cane usually like inside?
100674.e: A bamboo cane is usually hollow. It is divided into sections by joints.

100675.q: What is often made from bamboo in Asia?
100675.e: Bamboo is light, hard and grows back quickly. It is used to make chopsticks and baskets, for example.
100675.m: Many useful things are made from bamboo.

100676.q: Which part of bamboo can you eat cooked?
100676.e: Young bamboo shoots are popular in Asian cooking. They must be cooked before you eat them.
100676.m: Bamboo shoots are eaten only cooked.

100677.q: On which continent do especially many kinds of bamboo grow?
100677.e: Most kinds of bamboo grow in Asia, for example in China. Some kinds also grow in America and Africa.
100677.m: Asia is the continent of bamboo forests.

100678.q: How often do many kinds of bamboo flower?
100678.e: Many kinds of bamboo flower only very rarely, sometimes only after decades. Often all the plants of one kind then flower at the same time.
100678.m: Bamboo flowering is a rare event.

100679.q: On which continent does the African baobab grow?
100679.e: The African baobab grows in the savannahs of Africa south of the Sahara.
100679.m: The baobab is a tree of the African savannah.

100680.q: What is another name for the monkey bread tree?
100680.e: The monkey bread tree is also called the baobab. It is known by this name in many countries.
100680.m: The monkey bread tree and the baobab are the same tree.

100681.q: What does the baobab store in its thick trunk?
100681.e: The mighty trunk can store a great deal of water. That way the tree survives long dry seasons.
100681.m: The thick baobab trunk is a water store.

100682.q: Why do people say the baobab stands on its head?
a: Its bare branches look like roots
Its roots are up in the sky
It has no trunk at all
100682.e: Without leaves, the short, thick branches look like roots. That is why the tree looks as if it were standing on its head.
100682.m: The bare baobab looks like an upside-down tree.

100683.e: Baobabs are among the longest-living trees. Some are well over 1,000 years old.
100683.m: A baobab can live for over a thousand years.

100684.q: Where does the monkey bread tree get its name from?
100684.e: The tree's big fruits are called monkey bread. Baboons and other animals like eating them.
100684.m: Monkeys like nibbling the fruit of the monkey bread tree.

100685.q: When does the baobab lose its leaves?
100685.e: In the long dry season the tree sheds its leaves. That way it loses less water.
100685.m: Without leaves the baobab saves water.

100686.q: In which book does a character pull up young baobabs on his planet?
100686.e: In the book “The Little Prince” by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, the little prince has to pull up young baobabs. Otherwise they would burst his tiny planet.
100686.m: The little prince fights against baobabs.

100687.q: Although it looks like a tree, what is the banana plant really?
100687.e: The banana plant has no wooden trunk. Its false stem is made of tightly rolled leaves, so it counts as a herbaceous plant.
100687.m: The banana plant is not a real tree.

100688.q: Which way do bananas bend as they grow?
100688.e: Young bananas first hang downwards. Then they grow upwards towards the light and so become curved.
100688.m: Bananas are curved because they grow towards the light.

100689.e: Bananas are harvested green. Only as they ripen do they turn yellow and sweet.

100690.q: Which country sells the most bananas to other countries?
100690.e: Ecuador in South America is the biggest exporter of bananas. Many bananas in Swiss shops come from South America.

100691.q: What is no longer found in the bananas we eat?
100691.e: Wild bananas have lots of hard seeds. The bananas bred for eating only have tiny dark dots left.
100691.m: Eating bananas no longer have hard seeds.

100692.q: What happens to the banana stem after the harvest?
a: It dies and new shoots grow
100692.e: Each false stem bears fruit only once. After that it dies and new shoots grow from the ground.
100692.m: A banana stem bears fruit only once.

100693.q: Can you eat a plantain raw like a normal banana?
a: No, you cook or fry it first
Yes, but only with the skin
No, you only drink its juice
100693.e: Plantains are big and starchy. Raw they hardly taste of anything, so they are boiled or fried like potatoes.

100694.q: Which plant does the coconut grow on?
100694.e: Coconuts grow in bunches at the top of the coconut palm. This palm grows on tropical coasts.
100694.m: The coconut grows on the coconut palm.

100695.q: What is the clear liquid in a young coconut called?
100695.e: Young coconuts are filled with coconut water. It is clear and tastes slightly sweet.
100695.m: There is coconut water in a young coconut.

100696.q: How do coconuts get across the sea to other islands?
100696.e: The coconut has a thick, airy layer of fibres. That is why it floats and can drift across the sea to new beaches.
100696.m: Coconuts can float across the sea.

100697.q: What is the coconut really, to plant scientists?
100697.e: Botanically, the coconut is not a nut. Like the cherry or plum, it is a stone fruit with a hard stone.
100697.m: The coconut is a stone fruit.

100698.q: What is made from the fibres of the coconut?
100698.e: The tough fibres around the coconut are called coir. They are used to make doormats, ropes and brushes.
100698.m: Doormats are made from coconut fibres.

100699.q: How many dark “eyes” does a coconut have?
100699.e: At one end the coconut has three dark spots. The young shoot later grows out through one of them.

a: By pressing the flesh with water
By boiling coconut water for a long time
100700.e: For coconut milk, the grated flesh is mixed with water and pressed. It is not real milk.
100700.m: Coconut milk comes from the flesh.

100701.q: What does the Venus flytrap catch?
100701.e: The Venus flytrap catches mainly insects and spiders with its leaves. It then digests them.

100702.q: Which group of plants does the Venus flytrap belong to?
100702.e: The Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant. It gets nutrients from the animals it catches.
100702.m: The Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant.

100703.q: How does the Venus flytrap catch its prey?
100703.e: The trap leaves are built like two halves. If an insect touches them, they snap shut in a flash.
100703.m: The Venus flytrap's trap snaps shut.

100704.q: How many times does an insect usually have to touch the trigger hairs before the trap snaps shut?
100704.e: There are fine trigger hairs inside the trap. It usually only closes when they are touched twice in quick succession.
100704.m: Two touches set off the trap.

100705.q: In which country does the Venus flytrap grow wild?
100705.e: The Venus flytrap grows wild only in a small area in North Carolina and South Carolina in the USA.
100705.m: The Venus flytrap comes from the USA.

100706.q: Why does the Venus flytrap catch insects?
100706.e: The plant grows in wet bogs that are poor in nutrients. The insects give it important nutrients such as nitrogen.
100706.m: Insects are fertiliser for the Venus flytrap.

100707.q: How fast does the Venus flytrap's trap close?
a: In a fraction of a second
100707.e: The trap closes in less than a second. That is one of the fastest movements in the plant kingdom.
100707.m: The Venus flytrap snaps shut in a flash.

100708.q: What do the edges of the trap leaves have so that the prey cannot escape?
100708.e: There are long bristles on the edge of the trap leaves. When the trap is shut, they interlock like bars.

100709.q: Roughly how long does a trap stay closed for digestion?
